layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South Asian languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sound law. A phonological *change claimed or assumed to have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taken place in all forms that met the relevant conditions: *Grimm's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Law is an archetypal example. A term from the 19th century, linked

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the programme of the *Neogrammarians.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sound symbolism. The use of specific sounds or features of sounds

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a partly systematic relation to meanings or categories of meaning.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Generally taken to include: 1. The use of forms traditionally called

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *onomatopoeic: e.g. chiffchaff (warbler whose song alternates a higher

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a lower note). 2. Partial resemblances in form among words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: whose meanings are similar: e.g. among slip, slide, or slither, all with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: initial [sl}. In the second case the correspondence may be partly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: explicable by the nature of the sounds and meanings involved: e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: least sonorous vowel, [i), is often associated, in the vocabulary and in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the minds of speakers, with concepts of smallness. But in other cases

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it is a feature simply of a specific language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sound system. See phonological system.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: source. *Case role of e.g. the room in I left the room or from Sydney in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I hitchhiked from Sydney to Canberra.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'source feature'. Used by Chomsky and Halle, *SPE, of phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: features of *voice, *stridency, and *heightened subglottal pressure.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The classification of features into source features, *major class

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: features, etc. was said at the time to have 'little theoretical basis'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: source language. One from which a translation is made. E.g. if a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: poem is translated from German into English, German is the source

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language and English the 'target language'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South American languages. The indigenous languages of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effectively three main regions. Those surviving in the south of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: continent (roughly present-day Chile and Argentina) belong to a few

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: small families: Araucanian, in south-central Chile and a neighbouring

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part of Argentina, has the largest number of speakers. Those of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: central Andes (roughly from southern Colombia to south of Bolivia)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: include *Quechua(n), spread originally under the Incas, and *Aymará.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Those of the rest of the continent are genetically very diverse, some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: belonging to small families, others to larger ones distributed at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intervals over wide areas. The most important south of the Amazon

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is *Tupi-Guaranı, of which *Guaraní is, with Spanish, an official

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language of Paraguay. Gê, or a hypothetical enlargement 'Macro-Gê', is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another in the central area of Brazil. To the north and west the most

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important groupings are Panoan, in the headwaters of the Amazon,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Arawakan, *Cariban, and *Chibchan; the last group extends into

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the neighbouring part of Central America.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South Asian languages. The languages of the Indian subcontinent:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: see Indian languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South Caucasian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South Caucasian. See Kartvelian.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: South-east Asian languages. Variously classed as *Mon-Khmer,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which includes *Khmer (Cambodian) and *Vietnamese; *Tai, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes *Thai and *Lao; *Tibeto-Burman, which includes *Burmese;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also, among the many smaller languages, some belonging to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Austronesian, *Kadai (grouped with Tai as Tai-Kadai), and *Miao-Yao

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (= Hmong-Mien). The geopolitical area is part of a wider *Sprachbund,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the eastern Himalayas across to southern China, which includes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other related languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SOV language. One in which a *subject (3), *object (3), and verb are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at least basically or most commonly in that order. E.g., in the usual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: account, Latin: thus Caesar (S) bellum (O) gessit (V) ‘Caesar waged war'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. SVO language, VSO language, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: countries in Central and South America, from Mexico to Chile and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: some millions of native speakers in the USA.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Spanish. *Romance, the official language of Spain and of several

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Argentina, that were once part of the Spanish empire. There are also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: language, in poetry and prose, from the Middle Ages; carried

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Spain, to *Catalan or *Galician.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Originally the dialect of Castile in north Spain, and a literary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: southwards as the Moors were progressively driven from the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: peninsula, and overseas, by missionaries and colonists, after the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: European discovery of America. The term 'Castilian' is now used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of European Spanish, as opposed to Latin American; also, within

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spatial. Indicating or involving location in space. Thus here and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there are opposed in a system of spatial *deixis; under is a spatial

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (= locative) preposition in under the table.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SPE = The Sound Pattern of English, by Chomsky and Halle (1968). The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: classic account of *Generative Phonology; also the source for one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: widely used taxonomy of phonetic features.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker recognition. The recognition of the voice of an individual

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speaker, either by other people or automatically by a machine.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Spec. See X-bar syntax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: special clitic. One whose position in a sequence of elements is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: peculiar to it, or to it and to other clitics, and is not that which might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be expected from its role in the construction. Thus especially one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which appears in second position following *Wackernagel's Law.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dichotomy implies.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Opp. simple clitic. But the possibilities are more complex than this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: specialization. 1. Narrowing e.g. of word meaning; cf. restriction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of meaning. 2. Proposed *design feature of language: speech is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech processing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘specialized' in that there is no natural connection between its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: physical character and its consequences in the behaviour of speakers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Specified Subject Condition. A precursor, in the 1970s, of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky's proposed constraints on *bound (2) elements in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Government and Binding Theory.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Specifier (Spec). See X-bar syntax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spectrogram. A display of acoustic energy across a range of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: frequencies. In the form most helpful for the study of speech, changes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the distribution of energy over time are shown on the horizontal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dimension; frequency (typically from 1 to 4,000 Hz or cycles per

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second) on the vertical; and levels of energy, above a set threshold,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by a trace that intensifies as they increase.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from Latin speculum 'mirror'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speculative grammar. Style of philosophical grammar in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Middle Ages, in which the structure oflanguage, seen as in essence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: universal, is explained as mirroring that of reality. 'Speculative' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: question, and so on.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech act. An utterance conceived as an act by which the speaker

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: does something. Originally of *performatives: e.g. by saying 'I name

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this ship the Queen Elizabeth' a speaker will, in the appropriate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: circumstances, perform the act of naming it. Thence of utterances

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generally. E.g. in saying 'I will be there tomorrow' one makes a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: promise or a prediction: i.e. one performs an act of promising or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicting. If one says ‘Stephen is my brother' the act is that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: making a statement, if 'ls Stephen your brother?' that of asking a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A theory of speech acts was developed by J. R. Searle at the end of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the 1960s, on the basis of work by Austin. It included, among other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: things, a division of such acts into *representatives, *directives,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *commissives, *expressives, and *declarations.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech community. Any group of people whose language or use

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of language can be taken as a coherent object of study. Speakers of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English in general might be treated as such a community; also, e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speakers of a distinct variety that one might call ‘Birmingham

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English', spoken or usually spoken by part of the population of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Birmingham. So might any other population that meets some test of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coherence, whether large or small, bilingual or monolingual, in a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single place or scattered.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech error. An accidental error in speech: cf. slip of the tongue.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech island. A small speech community occupying an area

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surrounded by speakers of another language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech processing. General term covering processes posited in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minds of both speakers (in speech production) and hearers (in speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech synthesis

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: recognition). Thence of superficially equivalent processing by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: computers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: speech synthesis. Any artificial simulation of speech, e.g. as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: research tool in controlling stimuli for phonetic or psychological

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experiments, or in practical applications.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spelling pronunciation. A pronunciation of a word which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived from or influenced by its spelling. E.g. earlier ['fprıd] forehead

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has been widely supplanted by the spelling pronunciation ['f:hed].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'spell out'. To supply a *realization: e.g. a specific rule for English

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: might spell out a plural morpheme in its regular basic form (-(e)s).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spirant. An older term for a *fricative. Spirantization is a historical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: process by which a stop consonant becomes a fricative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: split. Change by which two distinct units, constructions, etc. develop

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from what was formerly one. Especially in phonology: e.g. Italian [k]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and [tS] (in amico ‘friend' vs. amici 'friends') are distinct phonemes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which have derived by a split, in Late Latin, from what had been a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single phoneme [k} (written c). Opp. merger.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: broke.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'split antecedent'. Two or more units which together supply the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: antecedent of a single *anaphoric element: e.g. Roger and his wife as the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: antecedent(s) of they in Roger told his wife they (Roger and his wife) were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: split ergative. (Language) in which agents and patients are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sometimes distinguished as in an *ergative and sometimes as in an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *accusative language. E.g. the 'ergative' pattern is found only when

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the verb is past or perfect, or the ‘accusative' only when the agent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and patient are pronouns.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: split infinitive. A form in English in which to and an uninflected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb, together seen as constituting an *infinitive, are separated by e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an adverb. Thus to and rid are ‘split' by systematically in to systematically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rid this town of layabouts. Traditionally proscribed under this name.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: split intransitive. The pattern exemplified in an *active language,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in which the single argument or valent of an *intransitive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction is identified in some conditions with the agent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a transitive construction and in others with the patient.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'split morphology hypothesis'. The view, held widely but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: challenged within *Lexical Morphology, that inflectional and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derivational morphology are in principle separate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'spontaneous'. (Sound-change) not explained by the phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context or the position in a word in which it takes place: e.g. the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: merger, in Southern British forms of English, of the vowel of moor and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: S-structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: poor with that of more and pour. Also described as unconditioned'; but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: there is no implication, at least in current theories, that such changes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: may not be explained, or seen as 'conditioned', by other factors.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spoonerism. Slip of the tongue in which parts of successive words

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are interchanged. Classic examples make sense in their turn: e.g. our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dear old queen' transposed to ‘our queer old dean’.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sporadic. (Sound-change) attested in some forms but not in others:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hence an exception, at first sight if no more, to the *Neogrammarian

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ‘regularity principle'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: families.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sprachbund. A group of languages, often of different historical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: origin, which are spoken in the same part of the world and have

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: developed similar structures. Classic examples include the *Balkan

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages and those of the Indian subcontinent; those of Southeast

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Asia or of the Meso-American group of *Central American languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are other striking instances involving members of several different

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of *convergence.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The area where such a group oflanguages is spoken is a linguistic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: area; the historical process by which they develop similar structures is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sprachgefühl. A linguist's intuitive feel for a language; cf. intuition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spread. (Lips) distended as in a smile: e.g. in the articulation of {i] in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Italian (dico or Dino). Opp. rounded.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vowel.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: spreading. The extension of a phonetic feature intrinsic to one

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: element to other adjacent elements. Thus in a word like maim the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: feature 'nasal', intrinsic to the consonants, spreads to the intervening

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: square brackets []. Mainly used: 1. To enclose phonetic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transcriptions: e.g. fish is phonetically [fif]. 2. To enclose syntactic or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other *constituents: e.g. wcnt into the garden can be analysed into the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: constituents [went [into [the garden]]}. Cf. labelled bracketing. 3. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representing phonological or other *features. Thus the vowel in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: scream has the feature [Front} or [+ Front], among others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: squish. J. R. Ross's term for an instance of *gradience.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: s-selection. Introduced by Chomsky in the 1980s for *valency or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *argument structure seen as determined by the meaning of an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: individual word. Opp. c-selection.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: S-structure. The least abstract level of syntactic structure in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Government and Binding Theory. Derived by successive modifications

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from the notion of *surface structure in transformational grammars

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the 1960s and 1970s; effectively jettisoned, with a similar relic of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *deep structure, in Chomsky's *minimalist programme in the 1990s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stacking

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stacking. Any pattern in which two or more units of a kind are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: independently related to the same element. E.g. in the man you saw who

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: kissed her who was here yesterday, three successive relative clauses are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stacked in relation to the single noun man.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: See also case stacking.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Stammbaum model. The model adopted especially by *Schleicher

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in the mid-19th century, in which historical relations among

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages are seen as like those between generations in a family tree

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (German 'Stammbaum'). Thus *Indo-European is represented as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parent language from which e.g. *Italic developed as one independent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: daughter language. Latin in turn is one independent daughter of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Italic, and the *Romance languages independent daughters of Latin.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Contrasted later in the century with the *wave model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: across a community or set of communities in which others are also

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standard. (Form, variety) which is learned and accepted as correct

layout_dets.text: exclamation) is distinguished by a rising tone () from He's DRuNK

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tone group. A stretch of speech identified as the domain of a unit of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intonation. E.g. Ill do it, but Ill need some help would normally have two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tone groups: Ill Do it / but Ill need some HELp. The division is shown by '

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and might or might not be marked by a *pause. Do is *tonic (shown by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: small capitals) in the first group, help in the second.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called a breath group, intonation group, intonational phrase,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: accent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tone language. One in which each syllable is characterized

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonologically by a distinct *tone or sequence of tones: e.g. Chinese.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thence, more generally, of ones in which most syllables are so

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: characterized, or most units of the lexicon, or in which contrasts of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitch have some lexical or morphological role. Thus, at the limit,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Norwegian is also conventionally called a 'tone language'. Cf. pitch

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: toneme. A unit of pitch, especially in *tone languages, treated as or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analogously to a *phoneme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tone sandhi. Phonetic modification of *tones, e.g. in Chinese, in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context of those on preceding or following syllables.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high vs. open or low.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tongue-body. (Features, etc.) distinguished by the position of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mass of the tongue within the mouth. E.g. front vs. back, *close or

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tongue height. See vowel height.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tongue root

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tongue root. The part of the tongue opposite the back wall of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: throat. Sounds articulated with the tongue root are called radical': e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *pharyngeal fricative as opposed to a velar or a uvular, which are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *dorsal or articulated with the dorsum.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tonic. (Syllable) which is prominent in a pattern of intonation. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Peter will finish any of Pe-, will, or fi- might be tonic: thus, with a tone

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that falls and then rises in pitch (), Peter will finish ('It's Peter who

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: will do it’), Peter "will finish ('He's definitely going to'), Peter will "Finish

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ('He won't give up before it's done’). In each case the tonic syllable,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and may also be longer.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished by small capitals, carries the main movement of pitch,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: examples, is one oftonicity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Also called the nucleus (or nuclear syllable): opp. atonic, non-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nuclear. A difference in the position of the tonic syllable, as in these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tonogenesis. The historical process by which *tone languages

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: develop from languages without tones. Thus, in one form of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tonogenesis, the pitch of a vowel might be lowered before a certain

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: class of consonants; these consonants are later lost, and from then

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on the pitch distinguishes these syllables from others.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: top-down. (Procedure) which determines the structure of sentences,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: etc. by working from larger units to smaller. Opp. bottom-up, e.g. as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alternative strategies for *parsing (2) systems, or as techniques for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analysing an unfamiliar language.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: topic. 1. Whatever a conversation, text, etc. is about. This might be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: identified explicitly (e.g. one speaker says 'I want to talk about x')

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or it might not. 2. A part of a sentence seen as corresponding to what

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the sentence as a whole is about: e.g. the topic of You can't buy clothes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at the supermarket might, in a specific context and with appropriate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intonation, be at the supermarket (‘One thing you can't do at the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: supermarket is buy clothes'). 3. A specific syntactic element whose

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: role is characteristically that of a topic (2); thus, in English, the phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which stands first in the construction of Cheap vodka you should never

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: drink or At the supermarket it might be cheaper.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Topics (1) are sometimes distinguished as 'discourse topics' as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: opposed to 'sentence topics'. For topic (2) cf. theme (1). In a language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: like English, topics (3) and subjects are distinct syntactic elements:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: topic[cheap vodka] subject[you] should never drink. But in languages of another

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: type, e.g. in Tagalog and others in the Philippines, the term 'topic' is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used in preference to ‘subject' of an element that has some but not all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the characteristics of a *subject (1) in the traditional European

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sense. In such cases, in particular, the remainder of the sentence is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: called the *comment.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: topicalization. The process of forming a derived construction in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which one element is a *topic (3): e.g. that of Beer I see as a necessity, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: topic beer, from that of the 'untopicalized'I see beer as a necessity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transferred meaning

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'topic-prominent'. (Language) in which the basic syntactic elements

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of a sentence are a *topic (3) and a *comment. Opp. subject-prominent.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: toponym. A place name: e.g. London.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'total accountability'. Principle by which, in an ordered series

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of *levels, all elements represented at a lower level must be related

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to elements at higher levels. E.g. each phoneme (at the level of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonology) must be a realization, or part of the realization, of at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: least one word or morpheme at the level of grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the object unraised, It is tough to meet these conditions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'tough-movement'. The postulated *raising (2) of an object from an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: infinitive construction that depends on an adjective such as tough. E.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that of these conditions in These conditions are tough to meet: compare, with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trace. A phonetically *null element said by Chomsky and his

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: followers to occupy the position from which a syntactic element has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been moved. E.g. in Mary I really love t, t is the trace left by a movement

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of Mary from its position in I really love Mary. Cf. empty category.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trachea. Anatomical term for the windpipe.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'trade language'. A *pidgin, *lingua franca, or other language,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used in commerce among people whose native languages are different.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: syntax.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'trading relation'. Used with reference to the balance between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different levels of description or different components of a grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Thus there are trading relations by which e.g. if the rules of phonology

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cover less the rules of morphology may in compensation have to cover

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more, or, by extending the scope of semantics, one may reduce that of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: best qualifiable.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'traditional grammar'. Usually of grammar as it was before the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advent of *structural linguistics, conceived as standing in a unified

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tradition going back to ancient times, with grammar in the 20th

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: century conceived as breaking away from it. Both conceptions are at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of phonemes.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transcription. Often in the sense of *representation. E.g. a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: phonemic transcription' is a representation of a form as a sequence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transderivational constraint. A restriction on a class of syntactic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derivations which refers to some factor outside those derivations: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to the possible role of a sentence in *speech acts. Proposed in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: context of *Generative Semantics in the early 1970s.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transferred meaning. A sense of a word or other unit which is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: derived by a shift from its basic field of reference to another. E.g. cold

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basically refers to physical temperature; but it has a transferred

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transfix

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: meaning in My reception was rather cold or She gave me a cold look. Cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: figurative.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transfix. A pattern of vowels or consonants seen as a non-continuous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: affix interleaved with a root or stem that is in turn not continuous: e.g.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the *patterns or pattern morphemes in Semitic languages.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transform. A sentence, structure, etc. derived by a *transformation:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: e.g. a passive sentence represented as a 'transform of’ an active.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transformation. An operation relating one set of structures,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: especially syntactic structures, to another. Thus, in many accounts,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the structures assigned to *declaratives such as She is here or You can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *interrogatives (Is she here?, Can you help me?).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: help me are related by a transformation to those of the corresponding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Transformations were developed by (Zellig) Harris in the 1950s as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operations relating one set of forms (e.g. phrases or sentences) to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: another. Also in parallel by Chomsky as operations on *phrase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structure trees deriving other phrase structure trees. In a standard

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: account a transformational rule (or T-rule) had two parts: a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: structural description or SD, which analysed the structures that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: could undergo the operation into two or more successive elements,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and a structural change or SC. which specified a derived structure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resulting from it. Thus the structure assigned to You can help me would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be divided into three parts: an initial noun phrase (you), an auxiliary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: verb (can), and the remainder (help me). In the derived structure of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponding interrogative the position of the first two would then be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: reversed: you can . .. → can you . . . In other cases transformations might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or might also involve the deletion of elements, or the addition of new

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ones, or *restructuring.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transformational grammar (TG). Any grammar in which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: different syntactic structures are related by *transformations. Thence

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: commonly, from the 1960s, of the theories of Chomsky, or of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Chomsky's school, in general.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In a transformational grammar as Chomsky first proposed it, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: main role of transformations was to relate the sentences of a language

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a whole to a small set of *kernel sentences. Its classic form dates

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from a reformulation by Chomsky in the mid-1960s. In this, a *base

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: component of a grammar generated a *deep structure for each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sentence. These structures were the input to a transformational

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: component, which was an ordered series of transformational rules;

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its output in turn was a set of *surface structures. The deep and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: surface structures of a sentence formed its 'syntactic description',

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which was 'interpreted' by further rules that supplied its *semantic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation and *phonetic representation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Theory.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For varying forms of such a grammar see Standard Theory, Extended

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Standard Theory, Generative Semantics; cf. Government and Binding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transparency

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transformational history. The sequence of transformations

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by which a sentence is derived in a *transformational grammar.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Represented in the 1950s by a 'transformation marker' or *T-marker.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transition. 1. Usually of transitions between successive speech

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sounds. Thus transitional *formants' are found e.g. in transitions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: between stops and vowels; 'transitional probabilities' concern the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: probability of one sound, or of one letter, following another.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Sometimes in a specific sense like that of *juncture: thus ‘close

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transition', 'open transition'. 2. See rheme.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'transition relevance place'. Term in *Conversation Analysis for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any point in a speaker's *turn, e.g. the end of a sentence, seen as a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: natural point at which another participant in a conversation might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: start speaking, or 'take the floor', instead.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transitive. (Construction) in which a verb is related to at least two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nouns or their equivalent, whose semantic roles are characteristically

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those of an *agent and a *patient: e.g. that of She (agent) carried him

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (patient). A transitive verb is one which takes or can take such a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: construction: thus carry, or carry in its basic sense.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: From Latin transitivus 'going across'. The original sense was that of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'transition' from a noun referring to one person' or participant (Latin

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: persona) to another. Opp. intransitive.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transitive preposition. A preposition in the traditional sense: i.e.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one such as in which is followed by a complement (in Melbourne). Cf.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intransitive preposition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transitivizer. An affix, etc. by which a transitive verb is derived

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from an intransitive. E.g., schematically, cup fell "The cup fell over';

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: I fell-TRAns cup 'I knocked over the cup'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'translation'. Introduced into French linguistics by L. Tesnière for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the process by which a unit that is basically of one syntactic class is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transferred to a role that is basically that of another. Thus cool is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: basically an adjective, and in and out are basically prepositions. But in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the cool of the night or the ins and outs they are 'translated' to the role of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nouns. A grammatical element is 'translative' if it is seen as marking

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a 'translation': e.g. the is translative in both these examples.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. transposition (2).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transparency. The degree to which a more *abstract representation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corresponds to one that is less abstract. Opp. opacity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A Transparency Principle was proposed by D. W. Lightfoot in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: late 1970s, as a factor explaining rapid change in syntax. In each

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generation, speakers were seen as *internalizing a grammar which,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: according to Chomsky's *Extended Standard Theory, included rules

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for both *deep (more abstract) and *surface (less abstract) structures

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of sentences. Over several generations, surface structures might

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transposition

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: change gradually, through stylistic shifts, contacts with other

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: languages, etc., while deep structures remained constant. But at some

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stage a required degree of transparency would be violated, and, to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: restore it, the next generation would restructure them.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transposition. 1. Change of sequence: cf. metathesis. 2. Sometimes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of processes that change the class of a unit: e.g. the formation of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: happiness is one in which an adjective (happy) is ‘transposed' to a noun.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Cf. translation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tree diagram. Any branching diagram in which different branches

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are connected only at a point of origin, and all are connected, directly

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a *phrase structure tree, a *dependency tree.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or indirectly, to one node which is the origin of the whole: e.g. a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 'family tree' which displays the *genetic classification of languages,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mathematics called ‘graph theory'.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A 'tree' is technically one type of 'graph' defined in the branch of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tri-. Prefix derived from the Greek word for 'three'. Thus a trisyllabic

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: word, or trisyllable, is one which has three syllables; a trigraph, such

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as German 'sch' for [S], is a sequence of three letters representing a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single phoneme. Opp. mono, di- or bi-, tetra-, etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cf. dual, paucal.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trial. Inflection, etc. used in referring to precisely three individuals:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: triangular. (Vowel system) in which a single open vowel is opposed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to closer vowels both front and back. Conventionally displayed on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sides of a triangle, as illustrated e.g. for Spanish.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A triangular vowel system

layout_dets.text: sentence, and marked as such in writing. In practice, words are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: elements (say, cant-a-v-o) is secondary.

layout_dets.text: zero (Ø). Usually of an element which is posited at some level of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: representation but whose realization is *null. Thus a noun phrase such

layout_dets.text: woman. *Relative clauses such as I saw in the men I saw are similarly said

layout_dets.text: zero anaphora. Relation in which a phonetically *null element is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seen as linked by *anaphora to an antecedent.

layout_dets.text: Thus, in English, an element such as he may be linked by anaphora

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: *Government and Binding Theory, a phonetically null *pro. Like he in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: English, this could then be anaphoric to Juan: thus, with the relation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shown by subscript *indices, Juan, dice que pro, viene.

layout_dets.text: morpheme when no allomorph is in fact present. E.g. in (three) sheep
